checkpoints: Unlike a pure server-to-server call the app controls end to end, the authorization-code flow round-trips through exactly one leg the app cannot vouch for itself: the user's browser.
Without state, the callback is just a GET request carrying a code — an attacker can deliver their own code into the victim's session, a CSRF attack on the callback.
That CSRF completes a login the victim never started — for instance logging the victim into the attacker's own identity, so everything that follows lands in the attacker's account.

state closes that loop: minted randomly at redirect, bound to the exact session that started that outbound leg, and required to match at callback, so the inbound leg can prove it is genuinely the answer to one specific outbound leg, not an arbitrary forged request.
Consuming state right after success (single-use) prevents an attacker who intercepted a valid state from replaying it later.
In the lesson, the mock branch calls the callback with no state at all — deliberate so the offline test runs clean — but that doesn't change the underlying rule.

In the real flow, the framework lets its strategy layer manage state; a hand-rolled callback that skips that check silently strips out the CSRF protection, which is a correctness bug, not an optional convenience detail.

This isn't a bug — it's a direct consequence of the design: AuthService.signIn signs role straight into the JWT alongside sub, and RolesGuard compares that claim against the route's @Roles O(1), deliberately never round-tripping the DB per request.

The 9am demotion only touches the DB, not the token already in the user's hands; that token still carries the signed role: admin, and the guard keeps trusting it until exp arrives, so the user still clearing RolesGuard at 11am is the guard doing exactly the job it was built to do, just trusting a claim that has gone stale.

Option one: a short-lived access token plus refresh-token rotation — at every rotation the server re-reads the role from the DB and signs a fresh access token, so staleness is capped at the access token's TTL; the cost is more refresh calls, and the window, while much shorter, is still nonzero.

Option two: a revocation list in a fast store (e.g. a Redis SET holding revoked jti or userId values, each with a TTL equal to the token's remaining lifetime so it self-cleans), checked by RolesGuard before trusting the claim, giving near-instant revocation the moment a demotion happens; the cost is exactly one extra fast-store lookup per request, a controlled slice of state re-introduced into a path designed to be stateless.

The senior call isn't 'always pick the safest option' — it's naming the staleness window the business actually tolerates: everyday role changes are well served by short TTL plus refresh rotation, cheap and sufficient; a demotion triggered by a compromised account or urgent security concern justifies paying for the denylist to get near-instant revocation.

Reverting to querying the role from the DB per request 'just to be safe' is the worst reflex, not option two's bounded cost: it throws away the entire benefit the claim-in-token design bought in the first place, erasing the very reason the role was signed into the token, just to dodge a problem a small, bounded mechanism already handles.
JWT verification only proves that a token was signed with a given secret and has not yet expired - it says nothing about which logical token type (access vs refresh) that token represents.

When `issueTokenPair` signs both the 15-minute access token and the 7-day refresh token through the same `jwtSecret()` call, the two tokens become cryptographically indistinguishable except for their `exp` claim.

`AtStrategy` and `RtStrategy` both configure `secretOrKey: jwtSecret()`, so a refresh token passes the access strategy's signature check exactly as a genuine access token would, since neither the payload (`{ sub }`) nor the verification logic encodes a token-type claim.
The root cause is the shared signing secret, not a logic bug inside either strategy's `validate()` - a single secret collapses the intended separation between access and refresh tokens.

Because the refresh token stays valid for 7 days instead of 15 minutes, this bug silently widens the effective leak/blast-radius window from minutes to a full week, defeating the short-TTL design intent of the access token.

The fix is to use two distinct secrets - one for signing/verifying access tokens and a different one for signing/verifying refresh tokens - so `AtStrategy` can only validate access-signed tokens and `RtStrategy` can only validate refresh-signed tokens.

As defense in depth, adding an explicit token-type claim (e.g. `type: "access" | "refresh"`) to the payload and asserting it inside each strategy's `validate()` prevents a future same-secret misconfiguration from silently reopening the same hole.

Verifying the fix means replaying the original exploit: the refresh token must now return 401 on the protected route while a fresh access token still returns 200, and `POST /auth/refresh` must still reject an access token - this cross-type case should be locked in as a regression test.

In NestJS, guards registered inside @UseGuards run strictly in the order they are listed, not in whatever order seems logically sensible — so @UseGuards(RolesGuard, JwtAuthGuard) actually executes RolesGuard first, before JwtAuthGuard ever runs.

RolesGuard reads req.user.role, but req.user is only ever populated by JwtAuthGuard after it verifies the Bearer token — so if RolesGuard runs before JwtAuthGuard, req.user is undefined for every single request regardless of what the client sends.

Because req.user is always undefined in this ordering, RolesGuard's check `!role || !requiredRoles.includes(role)` evaluates to true unconditionally and throws ForbiddenException for every caller — a valid admin token, a wrong-role token, and a missing token all collapse into the identical 403 response.

A request with no token at all never reaches JwtAuthGuard — the guard responsible for returning 401 on missing or invalid credentials — because RolesGuard short-circuits first with 403; the two symptoms (valid admin token still 403, and no token also 403 instead of 401) are two faces of the same misordering, not two separate bugs.

The underlying invariant is authentication before authorization: identity must be attached to the request (or the request rejected with 401) before any role or permission check can run, since authorization has nothing valid to compare against otherwise.

The fix is to swap the guard order to @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, RolesGuard), so JwtAuthGuard verifies the token and attaches req.user first — throwing 401 itself if the token is missing or invalid — and only then does RolesGuard compare the real req.user.role against the declared @Roles allow-list.

401 and 403 carry distinct meanings for client behavior: 401 means the caller is not authenticated and should re-login, while 403 means the caller is authenticated but not permitted and should not retry with the same credentials — running authorization before authentication collapses both into 403 and can mislead client retry logic.

The fix should be verified and locked in with a three-call status-code matrix — admin token → 200, valid token with the wrong role → 403, no token → 401 — kept as a regression test so a future guard-reordering mistake fails a test loudly instead of shipping silently.

A JWT signed with a hardcoded literal secret like `"secret123"` is only as trustworthy as that string; once it lives in source control, anyone with repo (or git history) access can mint a valid signature for any `sub` — including an arbitrary `isAdmin: true` claim — and walk through every `JwtAuthGuard` as that user. The fix is loading the secret from `ConfigService` or an env-backed secret manager, and because the committed value is permanently burned, it must be rotated immediately rather than just moved.

A JWT is a stateless credential verified purely by signature, so once issued there is no server-side switch to kill it before `exp` — a 30-day expiry means a single leaked token grants a full month of access with nothing the backend can do to stop it.

Because access tokens can't be individually revoked, they should be scoped to a short, minutes-scale lifetime; longer-lived sessions belong to a separate refresh token that carries its own revocation path instead of being baked into the access token's own expiry.

JWT payloads are base64url-encoded, not encrypted, so every claim packed into them — including a bcrypt password hash or an `isAdmin` flag — is plainly readable by anyone holding the token, whether a browser extension, a proxy access log, or someone pasting it into jwt.io.

Token payloads should carry the minimum needed to identify the caller, essentially just `sub` and `exp`; any other data a handler needs, such as email or admin status, should be looked up server-side from the verified user id rather than shipped inside the token itself.

Storing an access token in `localStorage` exposes it to theft by any XSS running on the page, since page-level scripts can freely read localStorage; an httpOnly, Secure cookie keeps the token out of reach of client-side JavaScript.

An effective PR security review ranks findings by real consequence rather than listing them in file order, pairs every finding with a concrete fix, and explicitly calls out what the code already does correctly — such as comparing passwords with bcrypt before issuing a token — so it reads as calibrated judgment rather than an unordered nitpick dump.

Claims about a token's safety are easiest to prove by demonstration rather than assertion: base64url-decoding a real issued token in the review thread shows the leaked fields directly, and codifying the fix as a CI check that the secret always comes from env (never a literal), plus a test asserting `exp` matches the intended policy, keeps the regression from coming back.

staleTime and gcTime answer two completely different questions — 'must I refetch?' and 'do I still have something to show instantly?' — and conflating these two questions is the root of every misunderstanding.
staleTime expiring does NOT remove data from cache: the entry simply turns stale, stays in cache, and keeps rendering as before.

Only the next trigger — a re-mount or a window focus — fires a background refetch while the screen still shows the old data: this is exactly stale-while-revalidate, isFetching = true while data is still there, so the Refetch button just flashes a Spinner instead of the list disappearing.
gcTime measures a completely different axis: it only starts counting once no component subscribes to that entry anymore (the query goes inactive).

Once gcTime expires, the entry is fully swept from cache, so the next mount has nothing to read — the component falls into isPending = true, renders a skeleton, and waits on a genuine request from scratch.
To reduce the background refetch chatter that flashes the Spinner, raise staleTime; to make returning to an old page show data instantly with no skeleton, raise gcTime.

The teammate raising gcTime hoping to 'refetch less' is tuning the wrong axis: refetching is decided by staleTime, while gcTime only decides how long an abandoned entry survives in cache — raising it never keeps data fresher for longer, it only delays how late an abandoned entry gets swept.
Summed up: fresh → stale → garbage-collected is one single line, and staleTime/gcTime are two independent markers on that same line.
invalidateQueries does exactly one thing: it transitions matching entries to stale — it deletes nothing and writes no data itself; the old list stays exactly as rendered until a fresh GET lands.
The moment an entry is marked stale, an active query — one currently rendered by some component — refetches right away.
An inactive query, with nothing mounting it at that moment, does not refetch immediately; it just waits for its next mount or next window focus to pull fresh data.

The mutation and the query genuinely know nothing about each other: useQuery(["users"]) only registers as a reader of the ["users"] cache entry, and useMutation's onSuccess only calls invalidateQueries({queryKey: ["users"]}) — no mutation needs to know which component is currently rendering, no component needs to know which mutation just ran.
queryKey is the shared address that makes this possible: every side only has to agree on the same key to cooperate automatically.
The full set of 'this mutation makes that query stale' relationships is the invalidation graph — every edge is a static declaration, not logic you run by hand.

That is exactly why both addMutation and deleteMutation reuse ONE single edge (both invalidate ["users"]) instead of each write needing its own splice/remove logic — the UI always converges to server truth through one refetch, with no manual state patching.

The failure mode sits precisely where the model leans hardest on: if the key doesn't match (e.g. invalidating ["user"] while the query is registered under ["users"]), the invalidation becomes a silent no-op, no error is thrown, the list simply sits frozen after the mutation — which is why keeping keys consistent (a shared constant or a query-key factory) matters far more than its surface simplicity suggests.
Names the swallowed error in createUser (try/catch returning null on any failure) as the most severe smell, because it produces a false success the user has no way to detect.
Explains the mechanism precisely: TanStack Query's error UI (isError/onError) only fires when mutationFn throws, so a resolved null is treated as success even though the request actually failed.

Identifies the second smell: addMutation.onSuccess and deleteMutation.onSuccess write their own guessed cache updates (Date.now() as id, input echoed back verbatim; manual splice/filter) instead of reading the server's actual response.

States the correct fix for the error-swallowing smell: createUser must throw on !res.ok (or propagate/rethrow network exceptions) and the component must wire isError/onError to surface a visible failure to the user.

States the correct fix for the cache-writing smell: replace the hand-written splices with onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["users"] }), or explicitly names the full optimistic-update pattern (onMutate snapshot/placeholder, onError rollback, onSettled reconcile) as the only acceptable alternative.
Articulates the underlying principle both smells violate: the server is the source of truth and the client cache should only mirror it, not fabricate or guess server-owned state.

Requires, before approval, a forced-failure test asserting the UI shows a visible error and the list has no phantom row, AND a create-success test asserting the row's id comes from the server (e.g. a follow-up GET) rather than Date.now().
Nothing here is architecturally broken — the QueryClient was created correctly with useState, so it survives re-renders.

The only missing piece is defaultOptions, so every query inherits the library default staleTime: 0, causing route changes and window refocuses to refetch data that barely changes (like a monthly catalog).

Before making any change, confirm the diagnosis by opening the Network tab or API access logs across a normal session and counting duplicate GET calls — dozens of identical responses for zero data change is the smoking gun, and it also reveals which queries are static versus genuinely live.
Fix at the right granularity, not with one blanket number: set a sane default staleTime (30_000) in defaultOptions.queries for data that changes at a normal pace.
Override staleTime specifically for ["countries"]/["plans"] to a value in the hours, and turn off refetchOnWindowFocus just for those two, since focus-sync buys nothing when the data barely moves.
Anything genuinely live keeps a short or default staleTime — this is a request-budget-versus-acceptable-data-age trade-off decided dataset by dataset, not a single app-wide setting.

Correctness survives the change because invalidateQueries after a mutation marks the entry stale regardless of staleTime, so a write to plans still refetches immediately; a long staleTime only suppresses refetch on read-only re-mounts and refocuses.

To prove the win, replay the identical session script before and after and diff the GET counts (dozens down to a handful), then re-run the mutation flow to confirm it still triggers an immediate refetch — this is a configuration change, not an architecture change.
Jank on fast scroll comes from the onScroll handler running on every scrolled pixel on the main thread and reading scrollTop/scrollHeight, forcing synchronous layout (forced reflow) mid-scroll.
Fix: replace it with an IntersectionObserver watching a bottom sentinel div (scroll box as root), which fires only when the intersection state actually changes, with no manual geometry math.
The first page must overflow the box (max-h-96) so the sentinel sits below the box's edge at mount, otherwise a load cascade fires the moment the component renders.
Duplicate requests happen because the bottom condition stays true while a page is loading, since hasNextPage hasn't flipped yet by the time the observer fires again.
Fix: gate the fetch with hasNextPage && !isFetchingNextPage right inside the observer callback before calling fetchNextPage().
Full-list re-renders come from {...u} giving every item a fresh reference on each render, defeating the identity check React uses to decide whether to re-render.
Fix: flatMap the cached pages untouched, without cloning, so old items keep their reference and stable keys and only the new rows mount.
Verify with the React Profiler (only new rows commit), the network log (exactly one request per cursor), and a scripted scroll e2e (10→20→25, has-next → no).
